claim: GPIHBP1 is a glycolipid-anchored membrane protein of capillary endothelial cells that binds lipoprotein lipase (LPL) within the interstitial space and shuttles it to the capillary lumen.
source: GPIHBP1 is a glycolipid-anchored membrane protein of capillary endothelial cells that binds lipoprotein lipase (LPL) within the interstitial space and shuttles it to the capillary lumen.
evidence: This is a statement of established function supported by prior research, as indicated by the context and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The LPL•GPIHBP1 complex is responsible for margination of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins along capillaries and their lipolytic processing.
source: The LPL•GPIHBP1 complex is responsible for margination of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins along capillaries and their lipolytic processing.
evidence: This statement describes the functional role of the complex, supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: GPIHBP1 comprises two functionally distinct domains: (1) an intrinsically disordered acidic N-terminal domain; and (2) a folded C-terminal domain that tethers GPIHBP1 to the cell membrane by glycosylphosphatidylinositol.
source: According to this model, GPIHBP1 comprises two functionally distinct domains: (1) an intrinsically disordered acidic N-terminal domain; and (2) a folded C-terminal domain that tethers GPIHBP1 to the cell membrane by glycosylphosphatidylinositol.
evidence: This claim is supported by biophysical measurements including HDX-MS, SPR, and structural predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: The acidic domain and the LU domain of GPIHBP1 serve different roles in regulating the kinetics of LPL binding.
source: We demonstrate that these domains serve different roles in regulating the kinetics of LPL binding.
evidence: This is supported by SPR kinetic measurements showing different kon and koff values for full-length vs truncated GPIHBP1.

claim: The acidic domain stabilizes LPL catalytic activity by mitigating the global unfolding of LPL's catalytic domain.
source: Importantly, the acidic domain stabilizes LPL catalytic activity by mitigating the global unfolding of LPL's catalytic domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing reduced unfolding of LPL in the presence of GPIHBP1 and activity assays.

claim: LPL is a triglyceride hydrolase secreted by myocytes and adipocytes that is essential for the lipolytic processing of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRLs) in the bloodstream.
source: For nearly six decades, we have known that lipoprotein lipase (LPL), a triglyceride hydrolase secreted by myocytes and adipocytes, is essential for the lipolytic processing of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRLs) in the bloodstream (Korn, 1955; Young and Zechner, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LPL-mediated processing of TRLs occurs along the capillary lumen.
source: LPL-mediated processing of TRLs occurs along the capillary lumen, and LPL is readily released from the surface of capillaries with polyanionic compounds such as heparin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LPL localization and function.

claim: LPL contains an N-terminal domain (NTD) for catalysis and a C-terminal domain (CTD) that is essential for lipid binding.
source: LPL contains an N-terminal domain (NTD) for catalysis and a C-terminal domain (CTD) that is essential for lipid binding.
evidence: This describes the known structural organization of LPL.

claim: LPL is active as a head-to-tail homodimer.
source: LPL is active as a head-to-tail homodimer, and several lines of evidence suggest that the CTD of one LPL monomer delivers triglyceride substrates to the NTD of the partner monomer (Kobayashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: The CTD of one LPL monomer delivers triglyceride substrates to the NTD of the partner monomer.
source: LPL is active as a head-to-tail homodimer, and several lines of evidence suggest that the CTD of one LPL monomer delivers triglyceride substrates to the NTD of the partner monomer (Kobayashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model supported by prior research.

claim: Certain LPL mutations (e.g., mutations in the catalytic triad or mutations that prevent LPL dimerization) markedly impair the processing of TRLs, leading to severe hypertriglyceridemia (familial chylomicronemia).
source: In the presence of certain LPL mutations (e.g., mutations in the catalytic triad or mutations that prevent LPL dimerization), the processing of TRLs is markedly impaired, leading to severe hypertriglyceridemia (familial chylomicronemia) (Brahm and Hegele, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by clinical and genetic evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: GPIHBP1 binds LPL within the interstitial spaces and transports LPL across endothelial cells to its site of action in the capillary lumen.
source: GPIHBP1 binds LPL within the interstitial spaces and transports LPL across endothelial cells to its site of action in the capillary lumen (Beigneux et al., 2007; Davies et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: In the absence of GPIHBP1, LPL does not reach the capillary lumen, and there is no margination of TRLs along the surface of capillaries.
source: In the absence of GPIHBP1, LPL does not reach the capillary lumen, and there is no margination of TRLs along the surface of capillaries (Goulbourne et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: GPIHBP1 is a member of the LU (Ly6/uPAR) protein domain family.
source: GPIHBP1 is a member of the LU (Ly6/uPAR) protein domain family, which includes CD59, SLURP1, C4.4A, TGF-β receptors, and uPAR.
evidence: This is a classification based on structural homology.

claim: The hallmark of the LU protein family is a three-finger–fold with a defined disulfide pairing motif involving eight highly conserved cysteines.
source: The hallmark of this protein family is a three-finger–fold with a defined disulfide pairing motif involving eight highly conserved cysteines (Ploug, 2003).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the LU protein family.

claim: A variety of loss-of-function mutations in GPIHBP1 have been encountered in humans with familial chylomicronemia.
source: First, GPIHBP1 function is tightly linked to human disease as a variety of loss-of-function mutations in GPIHBP1 have been encountered in humans with familial chylomicronemia (Beigneux et al., 2009; Buonuomo et al., 2015; Olivecrona et al., 2010; Plengpanich et al., 2014; Rios et al., 2012; Surendran et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple clinical studies as indicated by the citations.

claim: The majority of disease-causing mutations in GPIHBP1 impair the folding of the LU domain, leading to multimerized and dysfunctional GPIHBP1 molecules on the cell surface.
source: The majority of these disease-causing mutations impair the folding of the LU domain, leading to multimerized and dysfunctional GPIHBP1 molecules on the cell surface (Beigneux et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Several mutations in the CTD of LPL (e.g. C418Y) have no effect on catalysis but abolish the ability of LPL to bind to GPIHBP1.
source: Interestingly, several mutations in the CTD of LPL (e.g. C418Y, first identified in a patient with chylomicronemia) have no effect on catalysis but abolish the ability of LPL to bind to GPIHBP1 (and thus prevent LPL transport across endothelial cells) (Gin et al., 2012; Henderson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Among the entire LU protein family, only very few proteins have N-terminal extensions (e.g. GPIHBP1 and the spermatid marker SP-10).
source: Second, GPIHBP1 is unique from a structural perspective. Among the entire LU protein family, only very few proteins have N-terminal extensions (e.g. GPIHBP1 and the spermatid marker SP-10).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of LU protein family members.

claim: In human GPIHBP1, the N-terminal extension is highly enriched in acidic residues, with 21 of 26 consecutive amino acids being aspartic acid or glutamic acid.
source: In the case of GPIHBP1, the N-terminal extension is highly enriched in acidic residues, with 21 of 26 consecutive amino acids in human GPIHBP1 being aspartic acid or glutamic acid.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of human GPIHBP1.

claim: Early studies in cell culture suggested that GPIHBP1's acidic domain is important for GPIHBP1•LPL interactions.
source: Early studies in cell culture suggested that GPIHBP1's acidic domain is important for GPIHBP1•LPL interactions (Gin et al., 2008), but a detailed study of the functional impact of the acidic domain on LPL function has been lacking.
evidence: This is supported by prior cell culture studies as indicated by the citation.

claim: A large fraction of the GPIHBP1 produced by transfected mammalian cells is misfolded and in the form of multimers.
source: One of the impediments to progress is that a large fraction of the GPIHBP1 produced by transfected mammalian cells is misfolded and in the form of multimers (Beigneux et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: A secreted version of human GPIHBP11–131 was produced in Drosophila S2 cells as a fusion protein with uPAR domain III.
source: A secreted version of human GPIHBP11–131 was produced in Drosophila S2 cells as a fusion protein with uPAR domain III (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The GPIHBP1 protein was prone to an internal cleavage after Arg38 during enterokinase-mediated removal of the uPAR tag.
source: However, this protein proved to be prone to an internal cleavage after Arg38 during enterokinase-mediated removal of the uPAR tag.
evidence: This is an observation from the protein purification experiments.

claim: Arg38 in human GPIHBP1 is not conserved during evolution.
source: Alignments of multiple primate GPIHBP1 sequences revealed that Arg38 is not conserved during evolution.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: In GPIHBP1 from Nomascus leucogenys, which is 94% identical to human GPIHBP1, the residue corresponding to Arg38 is Gly38.
source: In GPIHBP1 from Nomascus leucogenys, which is 94% identical to human GPIHBP1, the residue corresponding to Arg38 is Gly38.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: Both GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 were purified to homogeneity and were monomeric with no traces of aggregation, as judged by analytical size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Both GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 (lacking the acidic domain) were purified to homogeneity by cation-exchange chromatography (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). Importantly, both proteins were monomeric with no traces of aggregation, as judged by analytical size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in the figure.

claim: The anomalous partitioning of GPIHBP11–131 during size-exclusion chromatography is most likely a consequence of a large Stokes radius caused by the presence of an intrinsically disordered N-terminal peptide.
source: The anomalous partitioning of GPIHBP11–131 during size-exclusion chromatography is most likely a consequence of a large Stokes radius caused by the presence of an intrinsically disordered N-terminal peptide (see next section).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the chromatography data based on the properties of intrinsically disordered proteins.

claim: GPIHBP134–131, which lacks the acidic domain, eluted with the expected hydrodynamic volume for a globular protein.
source: Consistent with this assumption, GPIHBP134–131, which lacks the acidic domain, eluted with the expected hydrodynamic volume for a globular protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data.

claim: The first 30–35 N-terminal residues in GPIHBP1 have a very high propensity for being an intrinsically disordered region.
source: We propose that the first 30–35 N-terminal residues in GPIHBP1 have a very high propensity for being an intrinsically disordered region (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on disorder prediction algorithms shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The disordered nature of the acidic domain is supported by the atypically large hydrodynamic volume of GPIHBP11–131 compared with GPIHBP134–131.
source: The disordered nature of the acidic domain is supported by: (1) the atypically large hydrodynamic volume of GPIHBP11–131 compared with GPIHBP134–131 (Figure 1C);
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data.

claim: The acidic domain is susceptible to limited proteolysis after Arg33 or Arg38.
source: The disordered nature of the acidic domain is supported by: (1) the atypically large hydrodynamic volume of GPIHBP11–131 compared with GPIHBP134–131 (Figure 1C); (2) its susceptibility to limited proteolysis after Arg33 or Arg38;
evidence: This is an observation from the protein purification experiments.

claim: The acidic domain exhibits extremely rapid hydrogen–deuterium exchange rates, with 100% deuterium uptake even after the shortest exposure time (10 s).
source: The disordered nature of the acidic domain is supported by: (1) the atypically large hydrodynamic volume of GPIHBP11–131 compared with GPIHBP134–131 (Figure 1C); (2) its susceptibility to limited proteolysis after Arg33 or Arg38; and (3) by the highly dynamic nature of the acidic domain as judged by extremely rapid hydrogen–deuterium exchange rates. In hydrogen–deuterium exchange/mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) studies, we observed 100% deuterium uptake in this domain even after the shortest exposure time (10 s) (Figure 1D and 1E),
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in the figures.

claim: The observed deuterium uptake in the acidic domain is consistent with the predicted deuterium uptake for a disordered GPIHBP11–33 peptide (87% after 1 s and 100% after 10 s).
source: which is consistent with the predicted deuterium uptake for a disordered GPIHBP11–33 peptide (87% after 1 s and 100% after 10 s).
evidence: This compares experimental data with theoretical predictions for disordered peptides.

claim: The deuterium uptake in the isolated LU domain in GPIHBP134–131 is indistinguishable from that of full-length GPIHBP11–131.
source: The deuterium uptake in the isolated LU domain in GPIHBP134–131 is indistinguishable from that of full-length GPIHBP11–131 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which implies that the acidic N-terminal region has little or no effect on the structure of GPIHBP1's LU domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data comparing the two constructs.

claim: The acidic N-terminal region has little or no effect on the structure of GPIHBP1's LU domain.
source: The deuterium uptake in the isolated LU domain in GPIHBP134–131 is indistinguishable from that of full-length GPIHBP11–131 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which implies that the acidic N-terminal region has little or no effect on the structure of GPIHBP1's LU domain.
evidence: This is an inference from the HDX-MS data.

claim: The conformation of the LU domain in GPIHBP11–131 was less dynamic when bound to LPL.
source: As documented by the heat maps in Figure 1D, the conformation of the LU domain in GPIHBP11–131 was less dynamic when bound to LPL.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data comparing free and LPL-bound GPIHBP1.

claim: The shift in dynamics of strands D and E likely reflects a transition to a state with increased secondary structure and/or a direct engagement in a ligand-binding interface.
source: This shift in the dynamics likely reflects a transition to a state with increased secondary structure and/or a direct engagement in a ligand-binding interface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: Individual alanine replacements of Thr85, Ser87, or Trp89 in β-strand D impaired LPL binding.
source: The fact that the HDX-MS analysis of GPIHBP1 identified β-strand D as a candidate binding interface for LPL was not entirely unexpected given that a previous mutagenesis study had shown that individual alanine replacements of Thr85, Ser87, or Trp89 in β-strand D impaired LPL binding (Figure 1E) (Beigneux et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by prior mutagenesis studies as indicated by the citation.

claim: Two missense mutations involving β-strand D (Ser87→Pro and Thr88→Arg) have been associated with chylomicronemia in humans.
source: Moreover, two missense mutations involving β-strand D have been associated with chylomicronemia in humans (i.e. Ser87→Pro [Buonuomo et al., 2015] and Thr88→Arg [Surendran et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by clinical genetic studies as indicated by the citations.

claim: Mutating residues within strand E of GPIHBP1 had little impact on LPL binding.
source: Mutating residues within strand E of GPIHBP1 had little impact on LPL binding (Beigneux et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by prior mutagenesis studies as indicated by the citation.

claim: The reduced deuterium uptake in strand E in the presence of LPL probably relates to a higher propensity for β-sheet formation in the setting of the GPIHBP1•LPL complex.
source: The reduced deuterium uptake that we recorded for strand E in the presence of LPL probably relates to a higher propensity for β-sheet formation in the setting of the GPIHBP1•LPL complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: The deuterium uptake in the intrinsically disordered N-terminal acidic domain did not change with LPL binding.
source: Interestingly, the deuterium uptake in the intrinsically disordered N-terminal acidic domain did not change with LPL binding.
evidence: This is an observation from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: The acidic domain either does not participate in the binding interaction or is involved in very transient binding events with LPL that do not lead to the formation of stable hydrogen bonds.
source: That finding suggests that the acidic domain either does not participate in the binding interaction or more likely is involved in very transient binding events with LPL (interactions that do not lead to the formation of stable hydrogen bonds).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: Residues 402–419 in the CTD of LPL are the most likely interaction site for the LU domain of GPIHBP1.
source: Comparing these states, we identified residues 402–419 in the CTD of LPL as the most likely interaction site for the LU domain of GPIHBP1 (shown in blue in the butterfly plot in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on differential HDX-MS data comparing LPL with and without GPIHBP1.

claim: GPIHBP11–131, but not GPIHBP11–33, attenuates the deuterium uptake in residues 402–419 of LPL.
source: This assignment is based on the fact that GPIHBP11–131, but not GPIHBP11–33, attenuates the deuterium uptake in this particular region (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: Two missense mutations in or close to residues 402–419 (C418Y and E421K) were identified in patients with chylomicronemia.
source: Two missense mutations in or close to this segment (C418Y and E421K) were identified in patients with chylomicronemia (Henderson et al., 1998; Henderson et al., 1996), and follow-up studies showed that both mutations impaired GPIHBP1 binding (Voss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by clinical genetic studies as indicated by the citations.

claim: Both C418Y and E421K mutations impaired GPIHBP1 binding.
source: Two missense mutations in or close to this segment (C418Y and E421K) were identified in patients with chylomicronemia (Henderson et al., 1998; Henderson et al., 1996), and follow-up studies showed that both mutations impaired GPIHBP1 binding (Voss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: GPIHBP11–33 reduced deuterium uptake in LPL peptides spanning residues 279–293.
source: Notwithstanding the more transient interaction, we did nevertheless observe that GPIHBP11–33 reduced deuterium uptake in LPL peptides spanning residues 279–293 (Figure 2B), which is localized in the domain interface between the NTD and CTD of LPL (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: Residues 279–293 of LPL are localized in the domain interface between the NTD and CTD of LPL.
source: Notwithstanding the more transient interaction, we did nevertheless observe that GPIHBP11–33 reduced deuterium uptake in LPL peptides spanning residues 279–293 (Figure 2B), which is localized in the domain interface between the NTD and CTD of LPL (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling of LPL.

claim: Residues 279–293 contain one of the heparin-binding sites in LPL enriched in basic residues (Arg281, Lys282, Arg284).
source: It is noteworthy that this region contains one of the heparin-binding sites in LPL enriched in basic residues (Arg281, Lys282, Arg284) (Hata et al., 1993) and therefore represents a potential binding partner for GPIHBP1's acidic domain.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on heparin-binding sites as indicated by the citation.

claim: Full-length GPIHBP11–131/R38G binds the CTD of LPL with a KD of 0.12 ± 0.04 µM.
source: Using this SPR setup, we found that full-length GPIHBP11–131/R38G binds the CTD of LPL with a KD of 0.12 ± 0.04 µM, whereas GPIHBP134–131/R38G binds with a KD of 1.41 ± 0.76 µM (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by SPR measurements.

claim: GPIHBP134–131/R38G binds the CTD of LPL with a KD of 1.41 ± 0.76 µM.
source: Using this SPR setup, we found that full-length GPIHBP11–131/R38G binds the CTD of LPL with a KD of 0.12 ± 0.04 µM, whereas GPIHBP134–131/R38G binds with a KD of 1.41 ± 0.76 µM (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by SPR measurements.

claim: The LPL CTDC418Y lacks the ability to bind GPIHBP11–131 or GPIHBPB134–131, even at concentrations as high as 1 µM.
source: When the LPL CTDC418Y was captured on immobilized mAb 5D2 (85 RU ~ 5 fmols/mm2), it lacked the ability to bind GPIHBP11–131 or GPIHBPB134–131, even at concentrations as high as 1 µM (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by SPR measurements.

claim: GPIHBP11–131/W89S has negligible binding to the CTD of LPL.
source: Consistent with those studies, the SPR measurements revealed negligible binding of GPIHBP11–131/W89S to the CTD of LPL (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by SPR measurements.

claim: The intrinsically disordered acidic domain of GPIHBP1 has little effect on the affinity of the LPL•GPIHBP1 interaction in the absence of a functional LU domain.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the intrinsically disordered acidic domain of GPIHBP1 has little effect on the affinity of the LPL•GPIHBP1 interaction in the absence of a functional LU domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SPR data for the W89S mutant.

claim: The 5–10-fold difference in the equilibrium binding constants between GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 could be accounted for by the differences in their association rate constants.
source: Kinetic assessment of the SPR binding data reveals that the 5–10-fold difference in the equilibrium binding constants between GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 could be accounted for by the differences in their association rate constants: kon = 1.04 × 106 M–1s–1 for GPIHBP11–131versus a kon = 0.10 × 106 M–1s–1 for GPIHBP134–131 (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of SPR data.

claim: The stabilities of the GPIHBP1•CTD complexes with GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 were essentially identical; both displayed koff values of 0.1 s–1.
source: In contrast, the stabilities of the GPIHBP1•CTD complexes with GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 were essentially identical; both displayed koff values of 0.1 s–1.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of SPR data.

claim: Removal of the single N-linked glycosylation in GPIHBP11–131 had no significant impact on the kinetic rate constants.
source: Removal of the single N-linked glycosylation in GPIHBP11–131 had no significant impact on the kinetic rate constants (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by SPR measurements on deglycosylated protein.

claim: The R38G mutation does not significantly affect the properties of the GPIHBP1 interaction with LPL.
source: The kinetics for the interactions between mAb 5D2-captured CTD or LPL and wild-type GPIHBP11–131 were similar to those measured with GPIHBP11–131/R38G (Table 1). Thus, the R38G mutation does not significantly affect the properties of the GPIHBP1 interaction with LPL.
evidence: This is supported by SPR measurements comparing wild-type and R38G mutant.

claim: The koff values for the LPL complexes with GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 were 5-fold slower than those for the corresponding CTD interaction.
source: The koff values for the LPL complexes with GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 were 5-fold slower than those for the corresponding CTD interaction, which indicates that GPIHBP1 forms a tighter complex with full-length LPL (Table 1, Figure 4B and 4C).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of SPR data.

claim: GPIHBP1 forms a tighter complex with full-length LPL than with the CTD alone.
source: The koff values for the LPL complexes with GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 were 5-fold slower than those for the corresponding CTD interaction, which indicates that GPIHBP1 forms a tighter complex with full-length LPL (Table 1, Figure 4B and 4C).
evidence: This is an inference from the kinetic data.

claim: The KD for the LPL•GPIHBP11–131/R38G interaction measured by microscale thermophoresis is 5.7 nM.
source: With this experimental approach, we determined a KD of 5.7 nM for the LPL•GPIHBP11–131/R38G interaction and a KD of 147 nM for the GPIHBP134–131/R38G interaction.
evidence: This is supported by microscale thermophoresis measurements.

claim: The KD for the GPIHBP134–131/R38G interaction measured by microscale thermophoresis is 147 nM.
source: With this experimental approach, we determined a KD of 5.7 nM for the LPL•GPIHBP11–131/R38G interaction and a KD of 147 nM for the GPIHBP134–131/R38G interaction.
evidence: This is supported by microscale thermophoresis measurements.

claim: LPL undergoes a time-dependent global unfolding of its catalytic N-terminal domain.
source: An intriguing finding in the current study was the observation that LPL undergoes a time-dependent global unfolding of its catalytic N-terminal domain, as judged by the loss of stable secondary structure in HDX-MS studies (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing bimodal isotope envelopes.

claim: The transition of LPL's catalytic domain into a pre-molten globule–like conformation provides a plausible structural explanation for the time-dependent decline in LPL catalytic activity at room temperature.
source: This transition into a pre-molten globule–like conformation of LPL's catalytic domain provides a plausible structural explanation for the time-dependent decline in LPL catalytic activity at room temperature (Osborne et al., 1985).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data in the context of known LPL instability.

claim: The unfolding of the catalytic domain in LPL proceeds with only one-half the rate of the parallel loss of catalytic activity.
source: It is noteworthy, however, that unfolding of the catalytic domain in LPL proceeds with only one-half the rate of the parallel loss of catalytic activity.
evidence: This is based on comparison of HDX-MS unfolding data and activity assay data.

claim: The unfolding of one LPL molecule in the homodimer would lead to the inactivation of both subunits.
source: That observation is consistent with a model where the unfolding of one LPL molecule in the homodimer would lead to the inactivation of both subunits.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the kinetic data.

claim: No changes were observed in the deuterium uptake of the CTD in LPL during prolonged incubations.
source: Of note, no changes were observed in the deuterium uptake of the CTD in LPL during the same time frame (Figure 6B), consistent with a greater stability of that domain (Gin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: The CTD of LPL has greater stability than the NTD.
source: Of note, no changes were observed in the deuterium uptake of the CTD in LPL during the same time frame (Figure 6B), consistent with a greater stability of that domain (Gin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and prior research.

claim: The acidic domain interacts with the domain interface of LPL (residues 279–290) in the setting of a mature GPIHBP1•LPL complex.
source: The fact that the acidic domain interacts with the domain interface of LPL in the setting of a mature GPIHBP1•LPL complex likely carries functional implications.
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS and cross-linking data.

claim: The stabilization of the catalytic domain of LPL by GPIHBP11–131 was primarily mediated by GPIHBP11–33.
source: Indeed, the stabilization of the catalytic domain of LPL by GPIHBP11–131 was primarily mediated by GPIHBP11–33 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS and activity assay data comparing different GPIHBP1 constructs.

claim: The stabilization of LPL's 'interdomain interface' by GPIHBP1's acidic domain serves to limit protein dissociation/unfolding of the partner monomers of an LPL homodimer.
source: We suspect that the stabilization of LPL's 'interdomain interface' by GPIHBP1's acidic domain serves to limit protein dissociation/unfolding of the partner monomers of an LPL homodimer.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the data.

claim: Certain homozygous missense mutations (LPLE410V, LPLG409R, and LPLS259R in humans; LPLG412R in cats) are associated with reduced LPL activity and chylomicronemia.
source: Certain homozygous missense mutations that are associated with reduced LPL activity and chylomicronemia [LPLE410V, LPLG409R, and LPLS259R in humans; LPLG412R in cats) (Foubert et al., 1997; Ginzinger et al., 1996; Kassner et al., 2015; Previato et al., 1994)] are located at the interdomain interface in close spatial proximity to the proposed binding site in LPL279–290 for GPIHBP11–33 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by clinical genetic studies as indicated by the citations.

claim: These disease-associated mutations are located at the interdomain interface in close spatial proximity to the proposed binding site in LPL279–290 for GPIHBP11–33.
source: Certain homozygous missense mutations that are associated with reduced LPL activity and chylomicronemia [LPLE410V, LPLG409R, and LPLS259R in humans; LPLG412R in cats) (Foubert et al., 1997; Ginzinger et al., 1996; Kassner et al., 2015; Previato et al., 1994)] are located at the interdomain interface in close spatial proximity to the proposed binding site in LPL279–290 for GPIHBP11–33 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and mapping of mutations.

claim: All disease-associated mutations at the interdomain interface alter the electrostatics of the interface.
source: All mutations alter the electrostatics of the interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the amino acid substitutions.

claim: Incubating LPL with peptides derived from GPIHBP1's acidic domain could promote stabilization of LPL, increase its conformational homogeneity, and enhance the likelihood of growing well-diffracting crystals for X-ray structure determination.
source: We suspect that incubating LPL with peptides derived from GPIHBP1's acidic domain could promote stabilization of LPL, increase its conformational homogeneity, and enhance the likelihood of growing well-diffracting crystals for X-ray structure determination.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the stabilization effects observed in the study.

claim: The intrinsically disordered and markedly acidic N-terminal extension of GPIHBP1 plays an important role in mobilizing HSPG-bound LPL within the interstitial spaces through long-ranged electrostatic interactions.
source: We propose that the intrinsically disordered and markedly acidic N-terminal extension of GPIHBP1 plays an important role in mobilizing HSPG-bound LPL within the interstitial spaces through long-ranged electrostatic interactions, thereby driving LPL into association with endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the biophysical properties of GPIHBP1 and kinetic data.

claim: An electrostatic 'encounter complex' is initially established between GPIHBP1's acidic domain and the basic residues in LPL's CTD.
source: Since the difference in kon for GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 is observed for both intact LPL and LPL's CTD alone, we propose that an electrostatic 'encounter complex' is initially established between GPIHBP1's acidic domain and the basic residues in LPL's CTD.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the kinetic data.

claim: The encounter complex guides the maturation of the interaction, facilitating a tighter binding interface between GPIHBP1's LU domain and residues 402–419 in LPL.
source: This encounter complex then guides the maturation of the interaction, facilitating a tighter binding interface between GPIHBP1's LU domain and residues 402–419 in LPL (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the kinetic and HDX-MS data.

claim: Cross-linking was documented between residues 1–33 of intact GPIHBP11–131 and Lys416, Lys424, and Lys430 in the CTD of LPL.
source: The cross-linking that we documented between residues 1–33 of intact GPIHBP11–131 and Lys416, Lys424, and Lys430 in the CTD of LPL is consistent with this initial encounter/maturation model.
evidence: This is supported by zero-length cross-linking experiments and mass spectrometry.

claim: The acidic domain plays little or no role in the stability of established GPIHBP1•LPL complexes.
source: Lending support to this two-step binding mechanism is the fact that the acidic domain plays little or no role in the stability of established GPIHBP1•LPL complexes.
evidence: This is based on the similar koff values for full-length and truncated GPIHBP1.

claim: The koff values for GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 are comparable, regardless of whether the binding is to LPL's CTD (koff = 0.1 s–1) or to full-length LPL (koff = 0.02 s–1).
source: The koff values for GPIHBP11–131 and GPIHBP134–131 are comparable, regardless of whether the binding is to LPL's CTD (koff = 0.1 s–1) or to full-length LPL (koff = 0.02 s–1).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of SPR data.

claim: A single molecule of GPIHBP1 binds one LPL homodimer in a 1:1 interaction model.
source: In the current study, the SPR data were obtained under more physiologic conditions (20°C in 0.15 M NaCl), and the binding profiles fit well to a simple 1:1 interaction model (i.e. GPIHBP1+LPL2⇆ GPIHBP1•LPL2).
evidence: This is based on SPR data fitting to a 1:1 binding model.

claim: Adding 10 mM EDC efficiently cross-linked LPL•GPIHBP11–131 in a 1:1 complex, consuming the majority of the LPL.
source: Adding 10 mM EDC efficiently cross-linked LPL•GPIHBP11–131 in a 1:1 complex, consuming the majority of the LPL (Figure 7, lanes 5 & 11).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE analysis of cross-linked samples.

claim: No covalent adducts were formed in the samples containing GPIHBP11–131 alone, LPL alone, or a mixture of LPL and GPIHBP134–131.
source: In contrast, no covalent adducts were formed in the samples containing GPIHBP11–131 alone, LPL alone, or a mixture of LPL and GPIHBP134–131 (Figure 7, lanes 3, 4, 6 & 10).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE analysis of cross-linked samples.

claim: Adding EDC to LPL in the presence of a 10-fold molar excess of GPIHBP11–33 led to the formation of a 1:1 complex with no evidence of higher-order adducts.
source: Adding EDC to LPL in the presence of a 10-fold molar excess of GPIHBP11–33 also led to the formation of a 1:1 complex with no evidence of higher-order adducts (Figure 7, lane 9).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE analysis of cross-linked samples.

claim: Each LPL molecule interacts with only a single acidic domain peptide.
source: These studies imply that each LPL molecule interacts with only a single acidic domain peptide.
evidence: This is an inference from the cross-linking data showing 1:1 stoichiometry.

claim: All but one of the five identified cross-links was established between LPL and GPIHBP1's acidic domain.
source: All but one of the five identified cross-links was established between LPL and GPIHBP1's acidic domain, consistent with the abundance of EDC-reactive carboxyl groups in the acidic domain.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of cross-linked peptides.

claim: The corresponding cross-linking sites on LPL included Lys298 in the catalytic domain and Lys416, Lys424, and Lys430 in the CTD of LPL.
source: The corresponding cross-linking sites on LPL included Lys298 in the catalytic domain and Lys416, Lys424, and Lys430 in the CTD of LPL (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of cross-linked peptides.

claim: One cross-linked peptide was identified between residues 100–125 (most likely Glu102) in the LU-domain of GPIHBP1 and residues 423–430 of LPL.
source: The one cross-linked peptide identified outside of the acidic domain occurred between residues 100–125 (most likely Glu102) in the LU-domain of GPIHBP1 and residues 423–430 of LPL.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of cross-linked peptides.

claim: No cross-links were detected between GPIHBP134–131 and LPL using 10 mM EDC for 90 min.
source: We did not detect cross-links between GPIHBP134–131 and LPL using 10 mM EDC for 90 min (Figure 7, lanes 6 & 10); however, we did observe such cross-links (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) if we drove the conjugation chemistry to higher yields by converting the o-acylisourea EDC intermediate to a more stable amine-reactive derivative (N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS)-ester).
evidence: This is an observation from the cross-linking experiments.

claim: Cross-links between GPIHBP134–131 and LPL were observed when using NHS-ester to drive the conjugation chemistry to higher yields.
source: We did not detect cross-links between GPIHBP134–131 and LPL using 10 mM EDC for 90 min (Figure 7, lanes 6 & 10); however, we did observe such cross-links (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) if we drove the conjugation chemistry to higher yields by converting the o-acylisourea EDC intermediate to a more stable amine-reactive derivative (N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS)-ester).
evidence: This is an observation from the cross-linking experiments.

claim: In GPIHBP1-deficient mice, the LPL in tissues is mislocalized to the interstitial spaces and never reaches the luminal surface of capillary endothelial cells.
source: In GPIHBP1-deficient mice, the LPL in tissues is mislocalized to the interstitial spaces and never reaches the luminal surface of capillary endothelial cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research on GPIHBP1-deficient mice.

claim: The LPL in GPIHBP1-deficient mice remains sequestered in the interstitial space, presumably bound to negatively-charged heparin sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs).
source: It is noteworthy that the LPL in GPIHBP1-deficient mice remains sequestered in the interstitial space, presumably bound to negatively-charged heparin sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) (Davies et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: The interaction between LPL and HSPGs is thought to be driven by electrostatic interactions and is characterized by fast kinetic rate constants.
source: This interaction is thought to be driven by electrostatic interactions and is characterized by fast kinetic rate constants (Lookene et al., 1996), presumably creating a dynamic reservoir of LPL within the interstitial spaces.
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: In wild-type mice, newly secreted LPL likely binds to HSPGs but then moves to GPIHBP1 on capillary endothelial cells.
source: In wild-type mice, newly secreted LPL likely binds to the same HSPGs but then moves to GPIHBP1 on capillary endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the known biology of LPL and GPIHBP1.

claim: The kinetic rate constants for GPIHBP1•LPL interactions are 10-fold faster for intact GPIHBP11–131 than for GPIHBP134–131 lacking the acidic domain.
source: This model for LPL mobilization by GPIHBP1 is consistent with the kinetic rate constants that we determined for GPIHBP1•LPL interactions, which are 10-fold faster for intact GPIHBP11–131 than for GPIHBP134–131 lacking the acidic domain.
evidence: This is based on SPR kinetic measurements.

claim: The importance of the positively charged heparin-binding sequences in LPL's CTD has been demonstrated by reduced binding of hLPLK403A;R405A;K407A;K413A;K414A to GPIHBP1.
source: First, the importance of the positively charged heparin-binding sequences in LPL's CTD has been demonstrated by reduced binding of hLPLK403A;R405A;K407A;K413A;K414A to GPIHBP1 (Gin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by prior mutagenesis studies as indicated by the citation.

claim: GPIHBP11–131 inhibited unfolding of the NTD of LPL.
source: GPIHBP11–131 clearly inhibited LPL unfolding (Figure 6C). This protective effect was predominantly due to the acidic domain because the GPIHBP11–33 peptide alone also attenuated LPL unfolding.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: The protective effect of GPIHBP1 on LPL unfolding was predominantly due to the acidic domain.
source: GPIHBP11–131 clearly inhibited LPL unfolding (Figure 6C). This protective effect was predominantly due to the acidic domain because the GPIHBP11–33 peptide alone also attenuated LPL unfolding.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data comparing different GPIHBP1 constructs.

claim: GPIHBP11–33 peptide alone attenuated LPL unfolding.
source: This protective effect was predominantly due to the acidic domain because the GPIHBP11–33 peptide alone also attenuated LPL unfolding.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: GPIHBP134–131 had a distinct but much less pronounced contribution on both unfolding rates and preservation of triolein hydrolase and esterase activity of LPL.
source: A distinct but much less pronounced contribution was provided by GPIHBP134–131 on both unfolding rates and preservation of triolein hydrolase and esterase activity of LPL (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS and activity assay data.
